claims.text: Stand in a split stance holding one dumbbell in both hands, both hands wrapped around the handle.

quotes.text: Stand in a split-stance position holding a dumbbell with both hands and wrap both hands around the dumbbell handle.

claims.text: Another common way to hold it is with both hands against the inside surface of the top plate.

quotes.text: Hold the weight overhead by grasping the inside dumbbell plate surface with both hands, or by grasping both handles of the kettlebell.

claims.text: Brace the torso, pull the shoulders down and back, and keep the head and neck in line with the spine throughout.

quotes.text: Stiffen your torso by contracting your abdominal/core muscles ("bracing"), and depress and retract your scapulae (pull your shoulders down and back), maintaining this position throughout the exercise.
Your head and neck should be aligned with your spine.

claims.text: Top position: arms vertical, elbows pointing forward and not completely locked, the dumbbell directly over the head.

quotes.text: Exhale and slowly press the dumbbell overhead, extending your elbows until your arms are vertical to the floor, elbows pointing forward, but not completely locked.
The dumbbell should be positioned directly over your head with your palms facing upwards and the dumbbell hanging vertically or angled slightly.

claims.text: Lower the dumbbell slowly behind the head without moving the upper arms; stop at about a 90-degree elbow bend or when the upper arms start to move back, and do not touch the back of the head.

quotes.text: Inhale and allow the weight to slowly bend your elbows, lowering the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner without moving your upper arms.
Continue lowering the dumbbell until your elbows reach a 90 degree bend or until your upper arms begin to move backwards. Be sure to avoid making contact with the back of your head.

claims.text: Keep the upper arms vertical and the elbows shoulder-width apart for the whole set.

quotes.text: Attempt to keep your upper arms vertical to the floor throughout the exercise and your elbows shoulder-width apart.

claims.text: Keep the head, torso, upper arms, wrists and feet still; only the elbows move.

quotes.text: Maintain your balance and avoid changing the position of your head, torso, upper arms, wrists and feet.

claims.text: Getting the weight into position is often the hardest part; use a weight you can get to the start position safely.

quotes.text: Depending on what type of resistance you use (dumbbell, kettlebell, band, etc.), sometimes the most difficult part is getting the weight into position. Use a weight that allows you to get to the starting position safely.

claims.text: If the weight is too heavy or you are tired you may arch the back, which strains the back and shoulder joints.

quotes.text: If the weight is too heavy or you’re fatigued, you may be tempted to arch your back, which can increase the strain on your back and shoulder joints.
Keep the speed of movement relatively slow, and avoid momentum to focus on your form.

claims.text: It can also be done seated on a bench with back support.

quotes.text: Sit on a bench with back support or stand with feet shoulder-width apart, core engaged.

claims.text: Listed common mistakes include flaring the elbows outward, swinging the weight with momentum, and locking the elbows at the top.

quotes.text: Flaring elbows outward
Using momentum to swing weight
Locking elbows at top

claims.text: A way out: a spotter is not usually needed, but for heavy sets one can help by supporting the elbows.

quotes.text: Spotting not typically required; assist by supporting elbows if needed for heavy sets.

claims.text: In an EMG study of the overhead dumbbell extension, the triceps long and lateral heads worked, most in the first and middle parts of the lift; the lowering phase needed less activity than the lift.

quotes.text: Eccentric phase elicited less muscular activity than concentric in both exercises.
Concentric contraction presented the same pattern during OD (long and lateral heads) and LD (lateral head). Initial and middle intervals elicited higher muscle activity than final interval.

claims.text: Across all weight training (not this exercise specifically), the most common way people were hurt badly enough for an emergency department was a weight dropping on them, and 90% of injuries involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: Triceps tendon ruptures are rare; they often follow a forceful lowering (eccentric) contraction or lifting against resistance.

quotes.text: Triceps tendon ruptures (TTRs) are rare and often occur as a result of falling on an outstretched hand, forceful eccentric contraction, direct trauma to the elbow, or lifting against resistance.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Tempo (up = pressing to straight arms, down = lowering): lower slowly and under control; ACSM advises moderate speed (1-2 s each way). Breathe in on the way down and out on the way up.

quotes.text: at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Inhale and allow the weight to slowly bend your elbows, lowering the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner without moving your upper arms.
Exhale and slowly press the dumbbell overhead, extending your elbows until your arms are vertical to the floor, elbows pointing forward, but not completely locked.

plate.viewWhy: The elbow bends front-to-back behind the head, and vertical upper arms (c6), the 90-degree stop (c5), the dumbbell clearing the head (c5) and a back arch (c9) all read side-on. Elbow flare (c12) is sideways. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: One dumbbell held vertically in both hands (census: dumbbell axis parameter). Standing split stance on the floor line (c1).
plate.start: Top position: split stance (c1), torso braced, shoulders down and back, head in line with the spine (c3); arms vertical, elbows pointing forward and not locked, dumbbell hanging vertically over the head (c4).
plate.end: Bottom position: elbows bent to about 90 degrees with the dumbbell behind, not touching, the head (c5); upper arms still vertical, elbows shoulder-width (c6); torso unchanged (c7).

checkpoints.label: Arms vertical
checkpoints.what: Upper arms stay vertical and still; only the elbows bend.

checkpoints.label: Braced torso
checkpoints.what: Core braced, shoulders down and back, head in line with the spine.

checkpoints.label: Stop at 90°
checkpoints.what: Lower to about a right angle, clear of the back of the head.

mistake.what: Back arching as the dumbbell is pressed up.
mistake.why: Healthline names it as what happens when the weight is too heavy or you are tired, straining the back and shoulders (c9).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks faults by frequency. Motra lists flaring the elbows first (c12), which is sideways and cannot be drawn from the side; the drawable back arch is shown.

plate.variantLine: Drawn standing in a split stance (ACE, anchor). A seated version on a bench with back support is also used (c11); the technique claims hold for both.

grip.type: One dumbbell held vertically in both hands, both hands wrapped around the handle (ACE). Holding the inside of the top plate is another common way (Healthline, c2); the drawing uses the ACE wrap because tier-A over-body rule C4 requires a wrapped thumb.
grip.width: Both hands together on the handle.
grip.handContact: Hands under the top plate, around the handle; the dumbbell hangs vertically over the head at the top (c4).

setup.step: Pick a dumbbell you can get overhead safely.
Stand in a split stance (or sit on a bench with back support).
Wrap both hands around the handle.
Brace, shoulders down and back, head in line with your spine.
Press the dumbbell overhead: arms vertical, elbows forward, not locked.

posture.point: Lower slowly behind your head to about 90°, without touching it.
Torso braced; do not arch your back.
Head, torso, wrists and feet stay still.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Arching the back to press the weight up.
handlingMistakes.fix: Brace; if the back still arches, use a lighter dumbbell.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Elbows flaring outward or upper arms moving back.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the upper arms vertical, elbows shoulder-width; stop lowering when the upper arms start to move.

rows.means: The triceps are doing the work.
Usually means the back is arching.
rows.fix: Brace and use a lighter dumbbell.

rows.means: Usually means the back is arching or the weight is too heavy.

rows.where: Sudden sharp pain at the back of the elbow while lowering

risks.risk: Dumbbell over the head: dropped weights are one of the most common causes of weight-training injuries; wrap both hands round the handle, lower slowly, keep it clear of your head, and pick a weight you can get overhead safely.
risks.riskNote: Kerr 2010 says the most common mechanism across all weight training; the wording here stays at "one of the most common" because the figure is not specific to this exercise.

risks.risk: Arching the back under a heavy weight strains the back and shoulders.
Triceps tendon ruptures are rare but can follow forceful lowering under load; add weight only in small steps (2-10%).

zooms.right: Both hands wrapped round the handle, dumbbell hanging vertically.
Upper arms vertical, elbows shoulder-width, dumbbell clear of the head at 90°.
zooms.wrong: Upper arms dropped back, dumbbell touching the head.
